figures.headline: Each step keeps only tokens the FSM accepts, so 'A' is masked at the start state while '.2' moves the machine to state 3.
citing_sentences: We illustrate the FSM sampling process in Figure 1 for the regular expression ([0-9]*)?\.?[0-9]*, which can be used to generate floating-point numbers.

abstract: In this article we show how the problem of neural text generation can be constructively reformulated in terms of transitions between the states of a finite-state machine. This framework leads to an efficient approach to guiding text generation with regular expressions and context-free grammars by allowing the construction of an index over a language model’s vocabulary. The approach is model agnostic, allows one to enforce domain-specific knowledge and constraints, and enables the construction of reliable interfaces by guaranteeing the structure of the generated text. It adds little overhead to the token sequence generation process and significantly outperforms existing solutions. An implementation is provided in the open source Python library Outlines (Louf and Willard, ).

sections.body: The paper addresses generating tokens from a language model so that the output matches a regular expression or context-free grammar. Common methods check the whole vocabulary at each step and set invalid token probabilities to zero, a fixed O(N) cost per token, where N is the vocabulary size. The proposed method uses the finite state machine form of a regular expression to start and stop guided generation and to build an index that gives the valid tokens at each step. The text states this costs O(1) on average. The approach is extended to context-free grammars and LALR(1) parsers. The section presents the index as an extension of existing regular expression libraries that does not modify their automata.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Constrained generation over a full vocabulary costs time per token, so the paper proposes a precomputed vocabulary index.

sections.body: A language model gives a probability vector over a vocabulary of size N, often on the order of 10^4 or larger, and tokens are sampled until EOS is found. Guided generation applies a boolean mask at each step so that only valid tokens keep nonzero probability. The text states that computing the mask is implicitly performed over all vocabulary elements and is easily the most expensive step. For regular expressions, the mask depends on previously sampled tokens. Partial matching from the start of the sequence costs at least linearly alongside the O(N) cost across the vocabulary. The section ends by asking how to match incomplete strings efficiently enough to compute the masks at each iteration.
sections.heading: LLM Sampling and Guided Generation
sections.headline: Masking invalid tokens each step means checking the whole vocabulary, so guided sampling cost grows with vocabulary size.

sections.body: The section frames regular expression matching as a finite automaton, so matching can stop and resume between samples without re-reading the sequence. Each vocabulary string is run through the FSM from every viable state (Algorithm 3), and the results build a map from FSM states to accepted vocabulary strings (Algorithm 4). A hash map makes the mask step O(1) on average, and index construction happens outside sampling. Memory scales with the number of states, |Q|, though not every state or string need appear. Example 1 walks through a floating-point number expression and a five-string vocabulary. A comparison with the Guidance library uses `max_tokens` and N=50,257. Its plotted results are in Section 3.2, which is not included in this text.
sections.heading: Iterative FSM Processing and Indexing
sections.headline: Indexing vocabulary strings by FSM state makes mask lookup constant time on average, with memory tied to the number of states.

sections.body: The section extends the approach from regular expressions to general parser-guided generation. A Python-like walk-through shows that after the partial string 'def f', the NAME pattern can continue, or the next token can begin with '(' (LPAR). Algorithm 4 would then map FSM states 0, 1 and 2 to the valid strings for NAME. To handle the parser, the authors use pushdown automata with a 6-tuple definition. They pair FSM states with parser states and terminal sets, and use the pre-image of the transition map to find stack values. For LALR(1) REDUCE operations, the index must be a trie to support queries on stack values. The section reports no measured results.
sections.heading: Extensions to Iterative Parsing
sections.headline: Extending the index to parsers pairs finite-state machine states with parser configurations, shown only through a Python-like example.

sections.body: The authors argue that the vocabulary index removes a run-time scaling barrier at the cost of memory. In their tests with a slightly augmented Python grammar, naively constructed indices were only around 50 MB. These indices were built from un-reduced DFAs, so redundant states could be removed, and NFAs are suggested as a lower-memory option. Other proposed uses are assisting training or fine-tuning when structured outputs are required, comparing masked and raw logits to evaluate models, and lifting masks into the model architecture to skip unneeded computation. These are proposals that the section does not test.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Naive indices stayed small in tests, and the authors suggest uses in training and lifting masks into the model.
